Today they use that same move of keeping the pattern and changing the world to plan their own story.","enduringUnderstanding":"Archetypal patterns such as the hero, the cautionary tale, and transformation live on because writers retell them in new settings, and the retelling can show what a culture values.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 24, students finish and revise their story and use compare/classify frames to explain how the retelling honors the original pattern while changing setting, details, or point of view.","performanceTask":"Shared Stories, Shared Lessons calls for crafting a narrative that adapts an archetypal pattern. Today's plan and opening draft become the foundation for that narrative."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"archetype","definition":"a pattern, character type, or story shape that appears again and again across many stories and cultures","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"retelling","definition":"a new version of an older story that keeps key ideas but changes details such as setting or characters","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"pacing","definition":"how quickly or slowly events move in a story","tier":"support"},{"word":"motivation","definition":"the reason a character acts the way they do","tier":"support"},{"word":"transition","definition":"a word or phrase that shows sequence or a shift in time or place","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Ch. 15, pp. 224–233 (review); homework Ch. 17, pp. 266–282"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Spark ideas by recalling how Riordan makes ancient gods feel modern, and connect that move to students' own stories.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"Gods in Modern Clothing","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"pp. 224–233"},{"type":"directions","text":"Look back at pp. 224–233, where Percy, Annabeth, and Ares talk about the Tunnel of Love, Hephaestus's traps, and Aphrodite. With a partner, name one way Riordan keeps something from the original myth and one way he changes it for a modern world."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What stays the same about Aphrodite and Hephaestus, and what is new in Riordan's version?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The old part is that Hephaestus sets traps and Aphrodite has a complicated relationship with Ares. The new part is that it happens at a modern place called the Tunnel of Love, and the gods talk like regular people with sarcasm."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Riordan keeps the pattern and changes the world around it. Today you will do the same thing: choose an old story pattern and plan a modern retelling that is yours."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to about 90 seconds of talking. Accept any reasonable comparison; the goal is to prime the idea of keeping the pattern while changing the setting."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Teach how expanded noun phrases, clear pronoun reference, and transitions help readers understand characters and sequence in a narrative.","activities":[{"id":"lab-language-study","title":"Precise Description and Clear Reference","minutes":10,"standards":["W.6.3","W.6.4"],"routine":"Language Study","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Narrative writers do two things to help readers: they add details to nouns, such as *a sarcastic god in a leather jacket* instead of *a god*, and they make sure every pronoun clearly points to one person or thing. Both choices show who a character is and why they act."},{"type":"directions","text":"Read each pair of sentences. Decide which is clearer and more vivid, and say why.

A. He told him to go because he was angry.
B. Ares, the furious god of war, ordered Percy to leave because Ares hated being challenged.

C. Percy walked into the arcade.
D. Percy, nervous and soaked from the rain, hurried into the flickering arcade."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"In sentence A, who is angry, and how can you tell? What does B fix?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"You can't tell who is angry because he could be Ares or Percy. B uses names and a description, so I know Ares is the angry one and I learn why."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do the added details in D tell us about Percy's feelings that C does not?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"D shows he is nervous and wet, so I can picture him and guess he is worried. C only says he walked."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Notice the transitions in a draft too. Words like *later that night*, *meanwhile*, and *suddenly* tell readers when time or place shifts. Try to use at least two today."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Model one revision aloud on the board: change 'She took it from her' into a version with names and a noun phrase. Students will revise their own sentences during drafting."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students notice how added details and clear pronouns make a sentence more precise.","sayAsk":"Say: You said the god was mad. We can say the furious god of war was mad. Frames: The ___ (adjective) ___ (noun) ___ (verb). ___, who ___, decided to ___. Ask: Who does 'he' mean in this sentence?","watchFor":"If students use only he/she/they, then prompt: Which name could replace this pronoun? If students add only one adjective, then prompt: Add where, when, or how with a phrase such as in the dark arcade. Success: student expands a noun phrase and fixes an unclear pronoun."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Expanding noun phrases","tryThis":"Give a simple sentence and a word bank of sensory adjectives. Have students add one adjective and one phrase, saying it aloud first."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask students to write a sentence where a noun phrase reveals a character's motivation, such as a hero desperate to prove herself."}]}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students plan a modern retelling built on an archetypal pattern (W.6.3.a, RL.6.9). Part B: Students begin drafting using dialogue, pacing, and description (W.6.3, W.6.4).","activities":[{"id":"lia-plan-story","title":"Part A: Plan a Modern Retelling","minutes":15,"standards":["W.6.3","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief","pages":"Ch. 15, pp. 224–233"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Archetypes are patterns that appear in stories everywhere. A hero story follows someone who faces a challenge and grows. A cautionary story shows a mistake and its consequence. A transformation story shows a character changed by what happens. Riordan's gods in Chapter 15 follow old patterns, such as Hephaestus's trap and the jealous love triangle, but live in a modern world."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete a story planner with these parts: (1) the original myth or pattern you choose (hero, cautionary, or transformation); (2) your new characters, with one expanded noun phrase for each; (3) your modern setting; (4) four key events: beginning, rising problem, turning point, and ending; (5) the central message you want to keep from the original."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which part of the original pattern will you keep, and which part will you change?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I'm keeping the cautionary pattern where someone is too proud and gets punished. I'm changing the setting from ancient Greece to a middle school robotics tournament, and the proud character is a team captain."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does your ending follow from what happens to your character?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The captain ignores his teammates' warning, his robot fails in the final round, and he learns to listen. The ending follows because his pride caused the failure."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.9"],"stem":"Based on pp. 224–233, which statement best describes how Riordan adapts a myth in Chapter 15?","choices":[{"text":"He keeps the gods' relationships and traps from the myth but places them in a modern setting with modern speech.","correct":true,"rationale":"Hephaestus's traps and Aphrodite's behavior come from the myth, while the Tunnel of Love and the casual dialogue are modern."},{"text":"He replaces the gods with ordinary humans who have nothing to do with the myth.","correct":false,"rationale":"The gods remain central; students may confuse the modern tone with a change in characters."},{"text":"He retells the myth exactly as in ancient Greece with no changes.","correct":false,"rationale":"Modern settings and dialogue show he changes details."},{"text":"He skips the myth and focuses only on Percy's quest.","correct":false,"rationale":"The dialogue explicitly references Hephaestus's traps and Aphrodite, so the myth matters to the scene."}]},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Circulate and check that each plan names a pattern, a modern setting, and a clear ending. Students who struggle can choose a pattern from the class chart: hero, cautionary, or transformation."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in explaining their story plan orally and adding details about time, place, and manner.","sayAsk":"Say: You said the story happens at school. We can say the story happens in a crowded cafeteria during lunch. Frames: My story is based on ___ pattern. It takes place ___ (where/when). In the beginning, ___. As a result, ___. Ask: Why did you choose this pattern?","watchFor":"If students list events without connection, then prompt: What caused the next event? If students are unsure of the pattern, then prompt: Is your character making a mistake, becoming a hero, or changing? Success: student orally states a pattern, a setting, and a beginning-to-ending sequence."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Choosing a pattern","tryThis":"Offer three familiar examples (hero overcoming a challenge, a proud character who fails, a shy character who becomes brave) and let students pick and adapt one."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Have students add a second archetypal element, such as a mentor or trickster, and explain how it supports the theme."}]}]},{"id":"lia-draft-story","title":"Part B: Begin Drafting","minutes":15,"standards":["W.6.3","W.6.4"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"A strong opening sets the scene and introduces a character quickly. Use dialogue to show personality, description to help readers picture the setting, and pacing to slow down at important moments and speed up in routine ones."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Here is how I begin: 'The gym smelled like old sneakers and nervous sweat. Maya, the tournament's youngest captain, gripped her robot's remote. "We can win this," she whispered.' I set the scene, introduce the character, and use dialogue in the first lines."},{"type":"directions","text":"Using your planner, write the opening of your story. Include a setting, at least one named character with an expanded noun phrase, a line of dialogue, and two transition words that show sequence or a shift in time or place. Check that every pronoun clearly points to one character. Write at least eight to ten sentences."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does your opening show who your character is and what they want?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I wrote that Jordan, a proud and impatient team captain, wouldn't listen to his friends. His dialogue, 'I don't need your help,' shows he wants to win alone."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Confer with students who start with a summary of events. Redirect them to a specific moment with a setting and a character speaking. Remind students they will finish tomorrow in Lesson 24."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in writing narrative sentences with added details about time, place, and manner.","sayAsk":"Say: You said he walked in. We can say he hurried nervously into the loud gym just before the match. Frames: ___, ___ (adjective) ___, walked ___ (where). Suddenly, ___. "___," said ___ (how). Ask: Where and when does this happen? How does the character feel?","watchFor":"If students write only simple sentences, then prompt: Add a where, when, or how phrase. If dialogue lacks speaker tags, then prompt: Who is speaking, and how? Success: student writes expanded sentences with at least one adverbial and clear dialogue."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Starting the draft","tryThis":"Provide a starter such as 'The ___ smelled like ___ when ___, a ___ (adjective) ___, ___.' Have students rehearse the first sentence aloud."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Challenge students to vary pacing by slowing down one key moment with sensory detail and speeding through a routine moment in one sentence, then explain the effect to a partner."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on how the archetype and modern details work together in their draft.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-turn-and-talk","title":"Keep the Pattern, Change the World","minutes":5,"standards":["W.6.3","RL.6.9"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Share your opening with a partner. Tell your partner which archetypal pattern you chose and one detail you changed to make it modern."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What did Riordan's modern gods teach you about retelling a story?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They showed me you can keep the old pattern, like a trick or a jealous love story, but give it new settings and funny, modern voices."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (Optional)","purpose":"Extend reading of The Lightning Thief to prepare for upcoming lessons.","activities":[{"id":"homework-ch17","title":"Read Chapter 17","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.9"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Read the summary of Chapter 17 (pp. 266 to the top of 274, ending with "…we turned our backs on the sea."). Then read and annotate Chapter 17, pp. 274 ("With some spare change…") to 282. Mark places where Riordan keeps or changes something from the original myths."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students review how Riordan modernizes divine characters in Chapter 15, then plan a short archetype-based retelling and begin drafting it with dialogue, description, pacing, and transitions. A Literacy Lab on expanded noun phrases and clear pronoun reference supports precise narrative writing.","keyActivities":["Launch Turn and Talk on what Riordan keeps and changes from myth","Literacy Lab on expanded noun phrases and pronoun clarity","Story planner for a modern retelling of a hero, cautionary, or transformation pattern","Quick Write drafting the story opening","Look Back partner share"],"vocabularyTaught":["archetype","retelling","pacing","motivation","transition"],"standardsCovered":["W.6.3","W.6.4","RL.6.9","W.6.3.a","W.6.3.b","W.6.3.c","W.6.3.d","W.6.5","L.6.1","L.6.3"]}}
